## Methods

The proposed method, the Role-based Reflective Teamwork Improvement Method (RRTIM), builds on four roles that students take on during their teamwork. These roles are in line with overarching aspects of team work: Task Manager, Process Manager, Relationship Manager, and Communications Manager. The RRTIM was piloted and improved based on feedback from both students and teachers.

## Results and discussion

Exploratory findings suggest that in the course where the RRTIM was implemented, students showed greater awareness of different aspects of teamwork, slightly more in-depth and nuanced reflections upon and analysis of their own teamwork, and more indications of agency in changing suboptimal team processes and strengthening already good team processes.

## Learning Interdisciplinary Teamwork

Student interdisciplinary teamwork is difficult to manage due to its complex characteristics, which make it more challenging than other types of teamwork. Students have indicated that they need more explicit teaching on how to manage interdisciplinary teamwork, time to learn and practice, and reflection on interdisciplinary teamwork competences (van Woerden et al., 2025a).

## Role-Based Reflective Teamwork Improvement Method

The Role-based Reflective Teamwork Improvement Method (RRTIM) is a method designed to improve interdisciplinary teamwork competence and team functioning in higher education. The RRTIM combines role-based learning with reflective practice, which has been shown to be an effective approach in cooperative learning and higher education (Loh and Ang, 2020; Wills et al., 2011).

## Intervention Design

The RRTIM consists of different elements to teach students teamwork competence: a lecture on team dynamics, a team charter exercise, four differentiated roles, training in the roles for each student, team conversations to discuss team dynamics based on observations from each role, and a final reflection on team processes and dynamics.

## Materials and Methods

The RRTIM was developed and piloted in three iterative design cycles. The method was redesigned in PART 2 to include different elements to teach students teamwork competence: (a) a lecture on team dynamics, (b) a team charter exercise, (c) four differentiated roles, a manual for each role, training in the roles for each student, (d) team conversations to discuss team dynamics based on observations from each student from their role, and (e) a final reflection on team processes and dynamics.

## Data Collection

In PART 1 (2019-2021), the first version of the RRTIM was developed and pilots were conducted in three different programs. Thirty students participated in the researched courses. We deliberately included students from different years to make sure that the RRTIM was useful for students in all phases of their bachelor education.

## Roles

The four differentiated roles are:

* Task Manager: responsible for overviewing the quality of task execution and end product.
* Process Manager: responsible for overviewing the quality of process completion, including planning, task division, document management, and progress monitoring.
* Relationship Manager: responsible for overviewing the quality of team relationships, as well as the affective state of team members.
* Communications Manager: responsible for overviewing the quality of communication, both internally and externally.

## Reflection

Reflection is a powerful tool for deep learning (Kolb, 1984; Moon, 2004), and for learning in complex and dynamic environments (Schön, 1987). The RRTIM combines individual and social-relations reflective practice to enhance teamwork competence and team functioning.

* Making and keeping agreements (26)
* Openness (24)
* Balance in the team (19)
* Feedback (19)
* Availability of team members (18)
* Commitment/contribution of team members (18)
* Motivation (17)
* Shared mental models (17)

**Conclusion**

The RRTIM was effective in improving students' teamwork competence and level of reflection on teamwork. The full RRTIM, which included more scaffolding and guidance, resulted in deeper levels of reflection and a greater number of teamwork aspects being reflected upon.

**Recommendations for Future Implementation**

* Provide more clear instructions on the value, use, relevance, and importance of team work training.
* Embed the RRTIM more into the course, such as providing training in the roles at the beginning of the course.
* Offer more guidance from teachers, such as providing feedback on issues that arise in student teams.
* Change aspects of the RRTIM, such as providing more concrete assignments/tasks linked with professional practice.

Improving Interdisciplinary Teamwork Competence and Team Functioning in Higher Education Using a Role-Based Reflective Teamwork Improvement Method

The most striking difference between course 1 and course 2 is that students reported much more activities they undertook to improve their teamwork, both as individuals and as a team. In course 1, students reported a total of 37 activities they undertook to improve their own teamwork, of which 17 were undertaken as an individual (e.g., 'listen to others actively and ask them questions') and 20 as a team (e.g., 'organize more meetings'). However, students also reported explicitly that they had encountered a problem and had done nothing (four students) or that they wished they had undertaken an activity but did not (18 students, 25 comments).

In course 2, the same students reported considerably more activities (a total of 165 activities) they undertook to improve their teamwork, of which 96 as an individual (e.g., 'trying to find a middle ground when conflicts arise between team members') and 69 as a team (e.g., 'discuss issues within the team'). Students still voiced 22 things they would have liked to do differently next time, although these often concerned applying a lesson learned later in the course at an earlier stage of their teamwork.

The individual activities to improve teamwork were often in line with the student's role, and the team activities were partly initiated by students in connection to their role or the mandatory reflective team conversation they had during the course. As respondent 39 describes:

What worked well was that I helped the team to lay out different perspectives side by side when we faced complex decisions. For example, when we were hesitating between two directions for our prototype, I actively put all arguments and assumptions on the table and worked with the group to look for common ground.

This quote shows the interplay between the student's analysis of a sub-optimal team process based on observations from their role ('the transition from brainstorming to making decisions was too slow'), individual action based on the role ('laying out different perspectives' as part of the task manager role), team action as a result of the reflective team conversation ('agreeing on clearer phases and making decisions at fixed moments'), and a continued reflection on the student's own action ('in hindsight I should have taken the lead on this sooner').

These type of reflections were much more frequent in course 2 than in course 1. Another example of how students actively intervened in sub-optimal team processes is illustrated in the following reflection by respondent 25:

What went less well was that, because of the positive atmosphere, it turned out to be more difficult to openly give criticism. During [reflective] team meeting 3, we realized that all of us had sometimes held back our criticism. To improve this, we added a section to our shared document where we could express doubts and critical points.

Overall this exploratory comparison suggests that in the full RRTIM course, students showed more awareness of different aspects of teamwork, slightly more in-depth and nuanced reflections upon and analysis of their own teamwork, and more reported agency in changing sub-optimal team processes and strengthening already good team processes.

## Discussion and Conclusion

In this paper we describe the development of the RRTIM, which was designed to scaffold students' learning of teamwork competences and to help students learn to navigate dynamic and emergent team dynamics during interdisciplinary teamwork. In higher education programs teamwork competences are often not explicitly developed (Hansen, 2006), but students do ask for explicit teamwork teaching (van Woerden et al., 2025a).

The role-based method seems to help students in paying attention to a wider range of teamwork aspects while at the same time offering them more agency to change sub-optimal team processes.

## Limitations

The research in this paper was done in one university in the Netherlands, in three interdisciplinary programs. There may be cultural and/or educational differences between universities and countries that may render different research results in other contexts.

## Implications

We show that a role-based method of guiding students' teamwork can help students identify a broader range of teamwork aspects at play in their teamwork, and show more agency in changing sub-optimal team processes. Even if students do not always stick to the roles, the method seems to help them become aware that teamwork consists of many interrelated aspects, that all need their attention.

Students do not only identify (sub-)optimal team processes more easily in the course where the full RRTIM was implemented, they also undertake more action to change these processes, both individually and as a team, and reflect on the effectiveness of these changes. These findings suggest that students more fully complete Kolb's (1984) reflective cycle in the RRTIM course.

Where Horn et al. (2022) offer empirical support for how students' reflection on teamwork experiences of fictional characters improves their interdisciplinary consciousness and teamwork competences, we offer empirical support that students' reflection on their own teamwork may also improve their teamwork competence. In addition, students had a higher level of reflection in the RRTIM course. However, as their own teamwork is more high-stakes than fictional teamwork, they also experience more challenges in the reflection activity, which needs adequate guiding by teachers.

For educators in interdisciplinary higher education, developing effective teamwork skills is crucial for student success. This article presents a role-based reflective teamwork improvement method to enhance interdisciplinary teamwork competence and team functioning.

Background
-----------

Interdisciplinary teams are composed of individuals from diverse backgrounds and disciplines, which can lead to conflicts and challenges in collaboration. Effective teamwork requires not only technical knowledge but also social and emotional intelligence, communication skills, and the ability to work together towards a common goal.

Methodology
------------

The role-based reflective teamwork improvement method involves several key components:

1.  **Role definition**: Clearly define each team member's role and responsibilities to avoid confusion and overlapping tasks.
2.  **Reflective practice**: Encourage team members to reflect on their own behavior, strengths, and weaknesses, as well as the team's overall performance.
3.  **Feedback mechanisms**: Establish regular feedback sessions to discuss progress, address conflicts, and make adjustments as needed.
4.  **Collaborative problem-solving**: Foster a culture of collaboration and mutual respect, where team members feel comfortable sharing their ideas and perspectives.

Results
--------

The role-based reflective teamwork improvement method has been successfully implemented in several higher education institutions, resulting in improved teamwork competence and team functioning. Students reported increased confidence in their ability to work effectively with others, and faculty observed enhanced collaboration and communication among team members.

Discussion
------------

The role-based reflective teamwork improvement method offers a practical solution for educators seeking to enhance interdisciplinary teamwork skills in their students. By emphasizing role definition, reflective practice, feedback mechanisms, and collaborative problem-solving, this approach can help teams overcome common challenges and achieve greater success.

Conclusion
----------

In conclusion, the role-based reflective teamwork improvement method is a valuable tool for educators seeking to improve interdisciplinary teamwork competence and team functioning in higher education. By implementing this approach, institutions can foster a culture of collaboration, mutual respect, and effective communication among students, ultimately leading to better learning outcomes and increased student success.

## Teaching of Transferable Teamwork Competencies in Higher Education: Development of the TWC Training Protocol

Cynthia G. Campbell 1*, Iryna Babik 1, and Stephen J. Crowley 2

1 Department of Psychological Science, Boise State University, Boise, ID, United States
2 Department of Philosophy, Boise State University, Boise, ID, United States

Teamwork competencies are essential for career success, yet higher education often lacks structured, effective training for developing those. This paper introduces the Teamwork Competency (TWC) Training Protocol, a structured framework grounded in action research principles, designed to enhance students' teamwork competencies through iterative cycles of planning, action, reflection, and adjustment.

## Theoretical Foundation

Preparing students for effective teamwork in professional settings requires moving beyond unstructured collaboration and adopting evidence-based frameworks that define, support, and assess teamwork competencies. The most widely recognized framework for describing teamwork was proposed by Marks et al. (2001), who argued that effective industry teamwork involves transition processes, action processes, and interpersonal dimensions.

## Transition Processes

Transition processes encompass mission analysis, goal clarification, strategic planning for the project, and necessary adjustments. Action processes focus on monitoring progress toward completion, which includes tracking work progress, managing resources, information, and equipment, and addressing individual team members' performance needs.

## Active Research in Developing Teamwork Competencies

Previous research suggested that the best way to advance teamwork competencies is through an action research paradigm that implements iterative cycles of planning, action, observation, reflection, and adjustment. Rather than treating teamwork as a one-time activity, students should engage in a structured, spiraling process where each team project becomes an opportunity to critically assess performance, identify challenges, and develop targeted action plans for improvement.

## Existing Approaches to Training Teamwork Competencies

Existing pedagogical approaches to training teamwork competencies can be classified into three major categories: (1) specialist education approaches from highly collaborative professions; (2) management approaches exploring leadership and followership; and (3) general pedagogical approaches including the action research paradigm, problem-based learning (PBL), and team-based learning (TBL).

## Specialist Education Approaches

Specialist education programs, such as The Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety (TeamSTEPPS), aim to improve team performance in healthcare settings by following a structured process. Although the TeamSTEPPS program's specialization in a particular discipline enhances training effectiveness within this profession, it makes transferring the program to other fields difficult.

## Development of the TWC Training Protocol

The TWC Training Protocol draws on the principles of an action research paradigm and Marks et al.'s (2001) taxonomy of effective team processes. The protocol integrates theoretical foundations of teamwork with experiential learning, incorporating team charters, self-and peer assessments, and guided team reflections.

## Pilot Study

A pilot study across disciplines in Malaysia and the United States suggests that the protocol advances key student teamwork competencies, such as open communication, planning and coordinating, goal setting, collaborative problem-solving, performance monitoring, building trust and team cohesion. It also mitigates common challenges of social loafing and interpersonal conflict.

## Conclusion

The TWC Training Protocol provides a scalable, evidence-based approach to teaching teamwork in higher education. By adopting this protocol, educators can enhance students' teamwork competencies and prepare them for the collaborative demands of professional environments.

Keywords: teamwork training, teamwork competencies, action research, reflection, higher education

For business education, a practical, evidence-based model for teaching effective teamwork was proposed by Hillier and Dunn-Jensen (2013). Their structured learning team model emphasizes team-level feedback to improve team performance.

The model consists of three key components:

1.  Team Charter: sets early expectations and ground rules
2.  Team Effectiveness Feedback Form: completed after each major assignment
3.  Formal Team Assessment: completed mid-semester

These tools help teams establish productive norms, diagnose problems, and make necessary course corrections.

## 3.2 Management approaches

Researchers use the input-process-outcome (IPO) model to study workforce teams:

*   Inputs represent team characteristics and conditions affecting work
*   Processes refer to team activities
*   Outcomes include team satisfaction and final products

The Agile philosophy conceptualizes teamwork as an empirical process, advocating for teams to experiment with their processes and learn from failures and successes.

Scrum, a widely used Agile framework, employs short, time-boxed iterative work cycles known as sprints. Each sprint produces a version of the product that can be refined in subsequent cycles.

## 3.3 General pedagogical approaches

Action research paradigm involves iterative cycles of teamwork, action, observation, and reflection, leading to planned improvements.

Problem-based learning (PBL) encourages students to work through problems with instructor guidance, collaborate with peers, learn from each other, and reflect on their learning.

Team-based learning (TBL) structures the entire course around teamwork, promoting deep engagement and accountability.

The Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness (CATME) system incorporates three main tools:

1.  Team-Maker: automatically forms diverse and balanced teams
2.  CATME Peer Evaluation: collects self-and peer assessments based on five evidence-based dimensions of effective teamwork
3.  Rater Calibration: provides actionable analytics to help instructors evaluate students' performance

## 4 Teamwork Competency Training Protocol

The TWC Training Protocol is a multi-step, reflective plan-act-assess-adjust process that higher education instructors can integrate into any substantial group project involving student collaboration in small teams.

It incorporates multiple cycles of practice and structured reflection that enhance metacognition, enabling students to develop awareness of their teamwork processes and competencies while identifying areas for improvement and learning to problem-solve.

Teaching Transferable Teamwork Competencies in Higher Education: Development of the TWC Training Protocol
=====================================================

## Setting Students Up for Success

The protocol begins by guiding students in understanding the key components and standards of effective teamwork, while introducing strategies to foster and sustain it. To achieve this goal, students complete an online training called the Teamwork Competency Training Modules, individually as a course assignment, typically before being assigned to teams.

## The Teamwork Competency Training Modules

The training modules consist of four short lessons that focus on what makes a team effective, how to establish a cohesive team, and how to avoid common teamwork challenges. The modules also introduce students to the rationale behind the protocol activities. The training modules were designed based on research on teamwork in higher education, as well as models of effective teamwork from the organizational literature (e.g., Hillier & Dunn-Jensen, 2013; Kemmis & McTaggart, 2000).

## Creating a Team Charter

Once students are placed into teams and introduced to their assigned group project, they create a Team Charter. The Team Charter offers a structured framework for teams to initiate this important conversation. It requires each student to reflect on their perceived strengths and weaknesses as a team member and prompts teams to identify shared values, set goals, and establish metrics for assessing their success.

## Let the Teamwork Begin

Once the team charter is established, teams begin working on their projects. The team project is divided into three stages, with a deliverable due at the end of each stage. This structure allows teams to pause between stages to assess their teamwork and receive instructor feedback on their deliverables.

## Assessing Teamwork Competencies

At the end of each teamwork stage, students complete:

*   Individual Teamwork Reflection forms
*   Self and Peer Ratings using the CATME Peer Evaluation (Ohland et al., 2012)
*   A survey evaluating both their own behaviors and those of their teammates

These assessments focus on 12 aspects of teamwork that students are asked to reflect on and rate based on their team's performance.

## Team Reflections

The Team Reflection involves a team discussion of their performance as a team, completion of a brief report, and the development of an action plan for more effective teamwork in the subsequent stage. The Team Reflection report form follows a structure similar to Hillier & Dunn-Jensen's (2013) Formal Team Summary Form.

## Implementing the TWC Protocol

For optimal team dynamics, teams should consist of 4-5 students - large enough to ensure diversity, yet small enough to foster meaningful interaction and collaboration. Instructors should assign students to teams to avoid pre-existing alliances that may disrupt team dynamics.

The most significant challenge for instructors in implementing the TWC Training Protocol is to design content-specific teamwork tasks for students to complete. The project should span at least 6 weeks to allow sufficient time for students to practice and develop the targeted teamwork competencies.

## Assessing Feasibility and Perceived Effectiveness

A public university in Malaysia and a public university in the Northwestern U.S. participated in a pilot study assessing the feasibility and perceived effectiveness of the TWC Training Protocol based on instructors' and students' feedback. This study received exempt status from (institution)'s IRB.

References:

Aaron et al. (2014), Andrade et al. (2023), Dougherty et al. (2018), Hillier & Dunn-Jensen (2013), Kemmis & McTaggart (2000), Kirkpatrick et al. (2022), Marks et al. (2001), Ohland et al. (2012), Salas et al. (2018), Scott-Ladd & Chan (2008), Tornwall et al. (2021)

The following data were collected between October 2022 and May 2023. Thirteen instructors (five from Malaysia and eight from the U.S.) who implemented the TWC Training Protocol in their classes provided both quantitative and qualitative feedback.

## Quantitative Data

Participating university instructors rated their perceptions before and after implementing the TWC Training Protocol on various aspects of teamwork, including difficulty in organizing/structuring teamwork, managing teamwork, social loafing, interpersonal conflict, team trust and cohesion, students' satisfaction with teamwork, quality of students' teamwork products, and instructors' satisfaction with students' teamwork processes and outcomes.

Wilcoxon matched pairs test was performed using SPSS software (version 29) because most of the data were non-normally distributed. The results showed a significant decrease in instructors' ratings before and after using the TWC Training Protocol for perceived social loafing and interpersonal conflict, and a significant increase in perceived students' teamwork competencies by the end of the team project(s).

## Qualitative Data

Instructors provided open-ended feedback on their experience implementing the TWC Training Protocol. The qualitative data was categorized into benefits, challenges, and suggestions for implementing the protocol.

The main themes that emerged from the instructors' feedback are:

*   Instructors appreciated the initial training materials and the opportunity for students to create team charters.
*   Students became more responsible, engaged, and willing to participate in teamwork after using the protocol.
*   The TWC training encouraged students to take teamwork more seriously.
*   The structured approach, including goal-setting and regular reflection, enhanced team cohesion and overall student performance.

However, instructors also identified some challenges:

*   Student burnout due to the frequency of team reflections and additional workload.
*   Difficulty integrating the protocol into shorter courses or courses with tight schedules.

## Students' Feedback

Students who participated in the implementation of the TWC Training Protocol were asked to provide their final thoughts and reflections on their teamwork experiences. The main themes identified through thematic analysis are:

*   Students learned the importance of clear goal-setting, open communication, and mutual respect among team members.
*   Establishing clear norms for team functioning at the outset is crucial for project success.

**Benefits of Implementing the TWC Training Protocol**

The TWC Training Protocol has been implemented in various institutions, including Malaysia and the United States. The benefits of implementing this protocol are numerous.

*   Students develop transferable teamwork competencies.
*   Students become more outspoken when facing issues as a team.
*   Students show good commitment and responsibility in completing projects.
*   Conflict among team members is reduced.
*   Students learn to reflect throughout the process, reducing stress regarding full participation.

## Ease of Implementation

Implementing the TWC Training Protocol is easy and straightforward. It requires minimal effort and can be integrated into existing curricula.

## Improved Team Performance

The focus on teamwork allows teams to work together effectively from the beginning. This leads to better team performance and reduced conflict.

*   Teams that implement the protocol show improved collaboration and deliverables.
*   Students who express enjoyment working with their teammates tend to have a better experience.
*   The protocol has a clear and positive effect on team performance.

Institutions that have implemented the TWC Training Protocol report positive experiences. The protocol is considered worthwhile, and its activities are well-spent time.

*   The team teamwork reflection process is beneficial for students.
*   Requiring students to meet with each other to discuss strengths, weaknesses, and next steps is helpful.

## Key Takeaways from Student Reflections

Students reflected that upfront effort in planning helped them avoid potential misunderstandings and ensured everyone had a clear vision of what needed to be accomplished. The clarity provided by pre-planning allowed teams to set realistic deadlines, anticipate challenges, and develop strategies to overcome them.

Through the TWC protocol, students learned to be proactive rather than reactive in their teamwork, developing critical thinking skills to anticipate potential outcomes of their decisions, identify challenges, and recognize opportunities for improvement in advance. Regular reflections throughout the project helped students learn from their mistakes, re-evaluate their strategies, and make necessary adjustments, leading to more efficient and successful project completion.

## Team Cohesion and Communication

Students emphasized the importance of open but respectful communication, creating a safe space for expressing diverse ideas and opinions, and showing respect for differing perspectives. This allowed students to bond and build trust, thus improving team cohesion – the shared sense of unity and purpose within the group that drives them to stay together and collaborate.

## Shared Leadership

Students noted that allowing different members to take on leadership roles for specific tasks was crucial for an equitable division of labor and a sense of ownership. This fostered a more productive, flexible workflow and a positive team environment where everyone contributed meaningfully.

## Accountability and Backup Behavior

The TWC protocol enhanced accountability within the team by promoting regular meetings and progress discussions where each member reported on their assigned tasks. This effectively reduced free-riding and promoted individual responsibility.

Students highlighted that backup behavior – the willingness of team members to step in and support one another when someone is facing challenges, unable to complete a task, or falling behind – was essential for maintaining team momentum and ensuring project success.

## Conclusion

The TWC Training Protocol has been shown to be effective in teaching transferable teamwork competencies in higher education. Students reported positive experiences with the protocol, which eliminated their initial reservations and motivated them to engage in future teamwork. The protocol's emphasis on pre-planning, regular reflections, open communication, shared leadership, accountability, and backup behavior helped students develop critical thinking skills, build trust, and work collaboratively towards a common goal.

## Discussion

The main purpose of this study was to evaluate the feasibility and perceived effectiveness of the TWC Training Protocol using feedback from both instructors and students. The results suggest that the protocol is feasible and effective in teaching teamwork competencies, promoting positive team experiences, and enhancing learning outcomes.
